Anjabar.web_botanical: Bistorta officinalis (syn. Persicaria bistorta, Polygonum bistorta)

uses_terms.meaning: abrasion or erosion of the intestinal lining

Anjabar.evidence_note: Traditional astringent use only; the sources found cite no clinical or pharmacological studies.

Attees Shireen.safety_note: Aconitum roots contain toxic diterpenoid alkaloids that can be fatal to the heart and nerves, with a narrow safe range; raw root is the main hazard and traditional processing is used to reduce toxicity. Use only as processed, professionally supplied preparations.
Attees Shireen.evidence_note: Traditional use with mainly preclinical research; no clinical trials found, and the species is IUCN Endangered.

uses_terms.confidence: unconfirmed (possibly OCR error for Nafkh-e-Shikam, abdominal bloating)

Bakayin.safety_note: Fruits and other parts contain meliatoxins (tetranortriterpenes); eating the berries can cause vomiting, diarrhoea, seizures and cardiac effects, and deaths have been reported.
Bakayin.evidence_note: Traditional use only; no clinical trials found, and the plant is mainly studied as a pesticide and for its toxicity.

Baobarang.safety_note: Animal studies show anti-implantation and antifertility effects (embelin) and fetal abnormalities in rats given high doses of a formulation containing it; reviewers advise caution in pregnancy and in children. No human safety data found.
Baobarang.evidence_note: Mostly preclinical research; one small children's study reported worm clearance, and reviewers call for clinical trials.

Basal.safety_note: Onions can cause contact allergy, dermatitis and, rarely, anaphylaxis in sensitive people.
Basal.evidence_note: Traditional use; no clinical evidence found for the seed uses listed.

uses_terms.meaning: weakness of the brain / cognitive weakness

Behman Safed.evidence_note: Traditional use only; no clinical studies found.

Behman Surkh.web_botanical: Salvia pratensis subsp. haematodes (syn. Salvia haematodes)

uses_terms.meaning: weakness of the brain / cognitive weakness

Behman Surkh.evidence_note: Traditional use only; Wikipedia coverage of this species gives no medicinal evidence, and the identity of red behen in Unani literature is not firmly settled.

Chanbeli.safety_note: Jasmine can cause allergic reactions and skin irritation; its effect during breastfeeding has not been adequately studied.
Chanbeli.evidence_note: Traditional use; the sources found describe fragrance and cultural use and cite no clinical evidence for the leaf uses.

Darchini.safety_note: Some cinnamon products are high in coumarin, which can harm the liver; stomach upset and allergic reactions occur, and it may interact with drugs processed by CYP450 enzymes and statins. Medicinal doses in pregnancy are not well studied.
Darchini.evidence_note: Mixed evidence for blood sugar and lipid effects; other traditional uses lack scientific support.

uses_terms.meaning: weakness of the brain / cognitive weakness

Funduq.safety_note: Hazelnuts are a tree-nut allergen and can trigger reactions from mild to severe anaphylaxis in allergic people (stated in the monograph; not confirmed by the Wikipedia pages fetched).
Funduq.evidence_note: Traditional use; no clinical evidence found for the listed Unani uses.

Heel Khurd.safety_note: Food amounts are fine, but medicinal amounts are not well studied in pregnancy and breastfeeding; the seed can trigger gallstone colic, so avoid larger-than-food amounts with gallstones.
Heel Khurd.evidence_note: Traditional digestive use only; reviewers rate the evidence for medicinal uses as insufficient.

Hummaz.safety_note: Rumex plants contain oxalic acid and some anthraquinones; reviews flag possible oxalate and anthraquinone-related adverse effects, though species-specific data were not found.
Hummaz.evidence_note: Animal studies show liver-protective and antioxidant effects; no clinical trials found.

Kababchini.safety_note: The constituent cubebin irritates mucous membranes; animal toxicity studies found no harm at tested doses but no human safety data exist. The monograph notes blood-pressure lowering and drowsiness with anaesthetic drugs.
Kababchini.evidence_note: Mostly lab and animal research; the only human report is a single case study, so clinical evidence is lacking.

Kalonji.safety_note: Amounts above food levels are considered likely unsafe in pregnancy because it may relax the uterus; it may lower blood sugar and pressure and affect clotting, and may interact with CYP2D6/3A4 drugs and warfarin. Topical oil has caused contact dermatitis.
Kalonji.evidence_note: Insufficient high-quality clinical evidence; small trials suggest possible benefit in asthma, arthritis and blood pressure, but results are mixed.

Kamila.safety_note: Dedicated human toxicity data are lacking; a rat study of seed extract reduced fertility hormones, and the powder is often adulterated. The monograph notes nausea. As a purgative it can irritate the gut.
Kamila.evidence_note: Traditional anthelmintic use; modern work is mostly preclinical and a review says anthelmintic activity still needs investigation.

Kaner.safety_note: Highly poisonous: contains cardiac glycosides such as oleandrin that cause vomiting, slow or irregular heartbeat and can be fatal, with deaths reported from teas made from leaves; sap irritates skin and eyes. Should not be self-administered.
Kaner.evidence_note: No clinical evidence supports the traditional uses; modern literature focuses on its toxicity.

Khar-e-Khasak Khurd.safety_note: Reports of stomach irritation and, in case reports, serious liver, kidney and nerve toxicity and priapism; may add to blood-pressure, diabetes and diuretic drugs, and pregnancy use is considered possibly unsafe. Prostate cancer patients should consult a doctor.
Khar-e-Khasak Khurd.evidence_note: Human trials show mixed or no effect on testosterone and athletic performance; evidence for stones is lab and animal only.

Khiyar Shamber.safety_note: Can cause nausea, vomiting, abdominal cramps and diarrhoea; the monograph advises avoiding it in pregnancy and lactation, and Ayurvedic texts discourage self-medication.
Khiyar Shamber.evidence_note: A small meta-analysis suggests partial benefit for childhood constipation, but the studies are few and at high risk of bias.

Khiyarzah.evidence_note: Traditional use only; no clinical evidence found, and the exact melon variety is not established.

uses_terms.meaning: abrasion or erosion of the intestinal lining
burning sensation in the kidneys / urinary tract

Khubbazi.evidence_note: Traditional demulcent use; European herbal authorities accept mallow flower for dry cough and mouth or throat irritation, but clinical evidence is limited.

uses_terms.meaning: weakness of the brain / cognitive weakness

Kishmish.safety_note: Calorie and sugar dense (about 65 g sugars per 100 g), so large amounts raise weight and blood sugar; raisins can cause kidney failure in dogs and cats.
Kishmish.evidence_note: A food with nutritional value; no clinical evidence found for the traditional medicinal uses listed.

Kulthi.safety_note: Raw seeds contain sugars that cause gas and diarrhoea and higher levels of trypsin inhibitors and haemagglutinins than most beans, so they need thorough cooking; the monograph lists indigestion, vomiting and bloating.
Kulthi.evidence_note: Traditional kidney-stone use rests on folk belief; no clinical trials found. The monograph names Vigna unguiculata, but Kulthi in Unani practice is horse gram (Macrotyloma uniflorum).

Lodh Pathani.safety_note: The monograph itself notes possible abdominal heaviness, nausea and constipation on an empty stomach. No independent safety data found in the sources fetched.
Lodh Pathani.evidence_note: Only taxonomy was confirmed from a stub page; no human clinical evidence was located.

Mainphal.safety_note: The monograph warns that excess may cause vomiting, indigestion and loss of appetite. The plant is described as having fish-poisoning and snail-killing properties; no detailed human toxicology was found.
Mainphal.evidence_note: Lab studies report antioxidant, anti-inflammatory, antidiabetic and lipid-lowering activity; no human trials were found.

uses_terms.meaning: roughness or hoarseness of the throat

Mauz.evidence_note: Wikipedia confirms its role as a staple cooked food; no clinical evidence for the listed Unani uses was found in fetched sources.

Mazoo.web_botanical: Quercus infectoria (galls induced by gall wasps)
Mazoo.safety_note: Reviews advise against long-term high-dose intake; the high tannin content can irritate the stomach and cause nausea and vomiting.
Mazoo.evidence_note: Reviews report mostly animal and lab findings (antibacterial, antioxidant, anti-inflammatory); human clinical evidence is very thin, with at most one clinical trial.

Mulsari.evidence_note: Wikipedia cites a 2012 review but reports no clinical findings; the fruit pulp is edible.

Muqil.safety_note: Memorial Sloan Kettering lists headache, nausea, belching, loose stools and rash; guggul may induce CYP3A4 (reducing some drugs' effect), may alter thyroid tests, and has been linked to liver enzyme rises. Pregnancy safety not established.
Muqil.evidence_note: Human evidence for cholesterol lowering is mixed, with several trials showing no benefit or raised LDL; evidence for arthritis and haemorrhoids is lacking. The species is critically endangered.

Neem Gum.safety_note: Neem oil can be toxic or fatal to small children; MSK describes serious poisoning from swallowed oil. Neem is reported to risk miscarriage and infertility and may lower blood sugar. These findings concern neem products generally, not specifically the gum.
Neem Gum.evidence_note: Wikipedia states there is insufficient clinical evidence for neem's medicinal benefits; the gum is mainly documented as a pharmaceutical excipient.

uses_terms.meaning: hysterical suffocation of the womb (uterine hysteria)

Ood-e-Saleeb.safety_note: No human safety data found; an extract showed no general toxicity in brine shrimp, which is only a preliminary lab signal.
Ood-e-Saleeb.evidence_note: Only lab findings (antioxidant, lipoxygenase inhibition) are reported; no human clinical trials were found.

Pambadana.safety_note: Cottonseed contains gossypol, which is toxic and was studied as a male contraceptive because it can suppress sperm production, sometimes irreversibly; the monograph itself lists miscarriage and infertility. This conflicts with its traditional use for low semen.
Pambadana.evidence_note: Gossypol research was abandoned as a contraceptive due to toxicity and irreversibility; no evidence supports the fertility-promoting traditional use.

Petha.monograph_botanical: Benincasa hispida Thunb, Synonym- Benincasa cerifera
Petha.evidence_note: Wikipedia notes mainly traditional Ayurvedic use and nutrition data; no clinical evidence for the seeds was found.

Pista.safety_note: Pistachios are a tree-nut allergen that can cause severe reactions including anaphylaxis; they contain urushiol-type irritants common to the cashew family and can be contaminated with aflatoxin.
Pista.evidence_note: An FDA qualified health claim says evidence suggests but does not prove nuts may reduce heart disease risk; reviews report modest blood pressure and triglyceride benefits.

Post-e-Gular.safety_note: The tree's milky latex can irritate skin. The monograph lists possible digestive-tract bleeding, sun sensitivity and rash, but I did not find independent confirmation.
Post-e-Gular.evidence_note: Wikipedia cites no clinical or pharmacological evidence for bark use.

Qinnab.safety_note: NCCIH lists impaired driving, dizziness and falls, risk of psychosis in predisposed people, cannabis use disorder, cannabinoid hyperemesis, lower birth weight with use in pregnancy, and risk to children from accidental ingestion. In many countries the plant is a controlled substance.
Qinnab.evidence_note: FDA has approved specific cannabinoid drugs for some rare epilepsies, chemotherapy nausea and HIV-related appetite loss; evidence for diarrhoea, haemorrhoids or cough is not established.

Qirfa.safety_note: Cassia contains coumarin, which can harm the liver at high or long-term intake and has a blood-thinning effect; European agencies advise limiting it. NCCIH notes possible interactions, skin irritation from oils, and caution with large amounts in pregnancy.
Qirfa.evidence_note: NCCIH says research does not clearly show cinnamon helps diabetes or weight loss; studies often fail to specify species or part.

Quaranful.safety_note: Eugenol is toxic at high doses in test organisms; oral use may cause problems in people with liver disease, clotting disorders, immune disorders or food allergies. Clove can irritate gums and skin.
Quaranful.evidence_note: Evidence supports clove oil containing eugenol for toothache and some dry-socket pain; evidence for blood sugar, fever and other uses is inconclusive.

Qurtum.safety_note: No specific safety findings found in fetched sources; the usual caution to check with a clinician before use in pregnancy or with bleeding problems is general advice, not sourced.
Qurtum.evidence_note: Small trials show safflower oil lowers LDL cholesterol more than butter or lard; no clinical evidence was found for the flowers or the Unani uses.

Qust.web_botanical: Dolomiaea costus (syn. Saussurea costus, S. lappa)
Qust.safety_note: A 2019 case report links the root to a severe pustular skin reaction (AGEP) confirmed by patch testing. The monograph lists dizziness and nausea. The species is CITES Appendix I.
Qust.evidence_note: Claims rest mostly on traditional use and preclinical work; the monograph file lists Orchis mascula (salep) but its elevation and root description fit costus, so identity was inferred from the name Qust, not confirmed against the book.

Shalgum.evidence_note: Wikipedia documents only culinary and agricultural use; no clinical evidence for the Unani uses was found.

Sumbul-ut-Teeb.safety_note: The monograph advises avoiding it in pregnancy, lactation and known hypersensitivity; I found no independent safety data. The species is critically endangered and CITES-listed.
Sumbul-ut-Teeb.evidence_note: Chemistry research is described as preliminary and medicinal claims are traditional; no clinical studies were found.

Tagar.safety_note: Data are for European valerian generally: may cause drowsiness, headache, dizziness and rarely liver toxicity; can add to sedatives; avoid in pregnancy and stop a week before surgery (MSK). Not specific to this species.
Tagar.evidence_note: Support is largely traditional; clinical trials of valerian for sleep are mixed and modest, and none specific to V. jatamansi were found.

Turanj.evidence_note: Historical uses such as seasickness and scurvy are described as supposed; a 2025 review notes antimicrobial activity of its compounds, with no clinical evidence found.

Zaqoom.safety_note: Euphorbia latex in general is a caustic skin irritant and poisonous; no species-specific toxicity data were found, so treat the latex as hazardous.
Zaqoom.evidence_note: Wikipedia gives no clinical evidence; only a purported snail-killing property and a link to the resin shilajit are noted.
